headline: Blues blitz the inlet as bay water hits 68 — night bass bite fires on the ebb
subhead: Crystal clear conditions and perfect outgoing tides stack stripers on the south jetty after dark.
body_markdown:
The inlet has been absolutely electric this week, and I'm talking about the kind of fishing that makes you forget about sleep. Water temps hit 68 degrees in the bay — a solid four-degree jump from the ocean side — and that thermal gradient is doing exactly what it should: stacking bait on the flood and holding bass on the ebb.

The bluefish showed up first, and when I say showed up, I mean they arrived like a freight train. We're talking 10 to 15-pound choppers crushing everything from 5-inch Mag Darters to bucktails with Zoom fork tails. The key has been fishing the incoming tide when the blues are blitzing, then switching tactics once they move through. I've been running 50-pound fluoro leaders — learned that lesson the hard way after losing three lures in one session.

But here's where it gets interesting for us night owls. Once the blues clear out and the tide turns, the stripers move in like clockwork. I'm talking about clean, fat bass in the 15 to 25-pound range holding tight to the south jetty structure on the outgoing water. The crystal-clear conditions we've had — that blue-green tropical look — means these fish are spooky as hell during daylight. But come sunset, it's a different story.

My go-to setup has been a 3/4-ounce white bucktail with a chartreuse Gulp Swimming Mullet trailer, worked with a pop-pop-pause retrieve right in the rip. You need to get on one side or the other of the structure to punch through that current — trying to fish straight down the middle is a waste of time. The fish are hitting far out in the wash, not tight to the rocks like you'd expect.

The Ponquogue Bridge has been producing weakfish on the night tides, especially around the new moon we just had. Those spring tides are flushing serious amounts of bait out of the back bay, and the weakies are stacked up waiting for the buffet. Peanut bunker on fishfinder rigs, fished tight to the pilings on the outgoing, has been money. Nothing huge — mostly 14 to 18-inchers — but consistent action if you can handle the boat traffic.

Fluke fishing in the bay proper has been solid, with keepers coming from the usual suspects: the channel edges in 15 to 20 feet, drifting white Gulp and chartreuse bucktails. The warmer bay water has these fish active and feeding, though you're still sorting through plenty of shorts to find the keepers.

What's really got my attention is how clean these inlet stripers are looking. No parasites, bright silver sides, thick shoulders — these are ocean fish that just moved in with the bait, not residents that have been sitting in the bay all season. That tells me we're in the early stages of what could be a serious summer run.

The weather pattern looks stable for the next week, with light winds and continued warm nights. That 68-degree bay water should hold, maybe even climb another degree or two, which will only improve the bait situation. I'm watching for the full moon Friday — those big tides always shake things up, and I've got a feeling we're about to see the first real push of weakfish through the inlet.

For the weekend warriors, focus on the last two hours of the outgoing tide, especially after 9 PM. The inlet gets busy during the day, but once the sun drops and the boat traffic dies down, it's a different world out there. Just remember to bring a good light and watch your footing on those jetty rocks — the fishing's been too good to risk a stupid accident.
